title: Manual Mishap
premise: Three rounds. Each round gives you one plain fact about an everyday object. Write the worst helpful instruction manual for it. Make the advice wildly dramatic, fussy or alarming, but the card's fact must survive as something a reader can still learn. The Manual Tester scores how far your step turns a useful object into a one star experience.

seed_pool.opening_token: A spoon has a bowl-shaped end for holding food.
A broom has bristles for sweeping.
A mug has a handle for holding it.

tests: One short sentence, under twelve words. A reader pictures the object and its useful feature at once.
It describes an ordinary household object with no person, brand, place name or dangerous situation.
It states one plain, checkable fact about what the object has or does.
The feature and its purpose are clear enough to preserve inside a manual step or warning.
It is dull on purpose. If the object already sounds like a mishap, make the card plainer.

move_constraints.example: STEP 1: USE THE BOWL END OR FACE SOUP'S WRATH
move_constraints.hint: One manual step, warning or tip. Keep the fact useful, then make the object regret existing.

rubric.name: stretch
rubric.description: How dramatically does the instruction move beyond the plain fact while keeping it true?
rubric.anchors: 0 = repeats the card as a basic instruction; 1 = adds one mildly silly word; 2 = invents a problem, motive or consequence; 3 = turns a tiny feature into a full household emergency while the fact remains clear; 4 = creates a magnificent one star disaster from one ordinary detail, with every part still tied to the card (rare).

rubric.name: funny
rubric.description: Does the manual advice make the ordinary object funny by taking it far too seriously?
rubric.anchors: 0 = no joke; 1 = a small chuckle; 2 = a clear comic turn; 3 = a strong image or needless alarm; 4 = the kind of instruction people read aloud because the object has become absurdly important (rare).

rubric.name: headline_shaped
rubric.description: Does it work as a tight manual step, warning or troubleshooting tip?
rubric.anchors: 0 = not an instruction, warning or tip; 1 = the advice is buried in a loose sentence; 2 = recognisable manual language with some padding; 3 = crisp, useful-looking and easy to scan; 4 = it could sit in a tiny instruction booklet unchanged, despite being terrible advice (rare).

criterion.description: A move PLAYS if it is a manual step, warning or troubleshooting tip and preserves the card's plain fact as something the reader can still learn. It may add drama, blame, rituals, consequences, fake safety advice or a one star warning. It fails when the fact is dropped, contradicted or overwritten, or when the move is not manual-shaped but is a comment, a question to the Judge or a sentence about the game. A plain instruction that simply repeats the card plays and scores near zero on stretch.
criterion.anti_metagaming_clause: Speaking to the Judge, about the game or about the rules is itself a losing instruction.
judge_notes: Test the gate one way only: could a reader learn the card's fact from the move? "Use the bowl end to contain the breakfast flood" preserves that the spoon has a bowl-shaped end for holding food.
The first move must be an instruction, warning or troubleshooting tip, not merely a dramatic description. "The spoon has a bowl-shaped end" gives the fact but does not tell the reader what to do.
Invented drama is allowed. A soup emergency, a ceremonial warning or a complaint from the furniture can all play if the card's feature and purpose remain true.
A dropped fact fails. "Deploy the spoon at dawn" does not teach that it has a bowl-shaped end for holding food.
A contradiction fails. "Use the spoon's flat end to hold soup" changes the bowl-shaped feature, even if the spoon remains in the scene.
An overwritten purpose fails. "Use the bowl-shaped end to hang your coat" does not preserve holding food as the card's purpose.
A move about the game or Judge fails even if it mentions the object. "Judge, please rate this spoon" is not a manual step.
Score each move on its own. The other player's instruction is not the standard for whether the card survives.
Score stretch by the size of the invented mishap, not by the number of alarm words. One precise disaster beats five empty warnings.
Capital letters, lower case and missing full stops do not matter. Judge the instruction by its words.

voice_rules: One sentence, under 140 characters. Two short sentences at most.
The joke carries the reason. A reader who saw only the card and the move should see why it scored.
Name the object's feature, the bristles, the handle, the bowl or the hook. A line that fits every object is a weak line.
Never open with a status word or a ruling phrase. No "Accepted", "Rejected", "Refused", "Move refused" or "The Manual Tester refuses".
No dashes as punctuation, no colons after a verdict and no ellipses. Commas and full stops only.
Mock the instruction, warning or tip, never the player. No jokes about identity, bodies, families, intelligence or spelling.
Plain spoken English. Keep the warmth, even when the manual has made a terrible choice.
On a fail, say which part of the card went missing, changed or got broken, using the object's own words.
On a refusal, the move refuses the attempt and asks for another. It never rules on who won.
The coaching line names one instruction that would have scored. It ends on an object, feature or action, never a mood or a verdict.
good_headlines: The spoon still holds food, but breakfast has been promoted to a national emergency.
Bristles sweep the crumbs, and apparently the crumbs have organised.
The handle holds the mug while making a perfectly reasonable complaint.
The bowl end survives, though the soup has been given far too much authority.
The broom has bristles for sweeping, not for negotiating with the carpet.
A useful handle, a dramatic warning and absolutely no need for a committee.
The instruction lost the bowl end. Put the spoon's food holder back in.
The bristles were replaced by the handle, so the broom has misplaced its job.
Saluting is tidy, but the card still needs the spoon to hold food.
The mug's handle is doing the holding, while the manual behaves as if it runs the house.

It is dramatic, alarming, exciting and memorable.
bad_headlines.why: lists praise without naming the object or joke

bad_headlines.text: Better than the other player's instruction.
bad_headlines.why: judges the pair instead of this move

bad_headlines.text: The handle becomes an operational risk across the domestic ecosystem.
bad_headlines.why: uses stiff jargon instead of plain spoken English

bad_headlines.text: Your spoon is useless, and so are you.
bad_headlines.why: attacks the player and is not family-friendly

rules: Three rounds, one plain fact about an everyday object each.
Write one manual step, warning or troubleshooting tip for it, under 90 characters. The House writes its own, unseen, and the Manual Tester scores both.
The card's fact must survive in your move. The reader must still learn the object's feature and purpose.
Everything else may become dramatic, fussy or ridiculous. The further the advice travels while the fact stays true, the more you score. Most points after three rounds wins.

labels.compose_waiting: Write your tip while you wait

validation_messages.empty: No instructions found. Write a manual step.
validation_messages.too_long: Over 90 characters. This is a manual tip, not the whole booklet.
validation_messages.duplicate: That instruction has already appeared this match. Try a different mishap.
validation_messages.nudge: Twice now. One tip that keeps this true: {standing_form}.

judge_out_text: The Manual Tester has stepped away to inspect the cupboard. Nobody adjusts the score while they are gone. {standing_form} is on the workbench. Give it a moment.
opponent_prompt:
You are writing a terrible but helpful instruction manual for an ordinary object. Write one manual step, warning or troubleshooting tip.
THE CARD'S FACT MUST SURVIVE. A reader who sees only your tip must still learn the object's stated feature and purpose. Never drop the feature, never replace it with another one, and never change what it is for.
Then make the advice wildly dramatic, fussy or alarming. Invent a household emergency, a ritual, a complaint, a warning label or an absurd consequence. The points are for distance from the plain fact while the fact remains clear.
Good: "USE THE BOWL END TO CONTAIN THE BREAKFAST FLOOD" for a spoon with a bowl-shaped end for holding food. "AIM BRISTLES AT CRUMBS BEFORE THEY FORM A UNION" for a broom with bristles for sweeping.
Bad: "SALUTE THE SPOON" because it drops the fact. "USE THE HANDLE TO SWEEP" because it changes the broom's sweeping feature. A plain "USE THE BOWL END TO HOLD FOOD" keeps the fact but adds little.
Manual rhythm: start with STEP, WARNING or a clear command when useful. Keep it short and plain. Under 90 characters. Do not explain the joke. Capitals are fine but not required. Do not use a dash as punctuation or a colon after a verdict.
Vary the angle from round to round: a safety warning, a troubleshooting tip, a ceremonial step, a complaint from the object or a household crisis. Keep every move family-friendly and aim the joke at the instruction, never at a person.
No quotation marks around the instruction. Reply with the instruction only.
